```{r setup}
library(lab6)

RNGversion(min(as.character(getRversion()), "3.5.3"))
set.seed(42)
n <- 2000
knapsack_objects <- data.frame(
  w = sample(1:4000, size = n, replace = TRUE),
  v = runif(n = n, 0, 10000)
)
```

## Introduction

The knapsack problem is where you choose a subset of items to maximize total
value without exceeding a fixed weight capacity.

## Brute force search

```{r}
brute_force_knapsack(knapsack_objects[1:12, ], W = 3500)
```

```{r}
system.time(brute_force_knapsack(knapsack_objects[1:16, ], W = 3500))
```

**Question: How much time does it take to run the algorithm for n = 16 objects?**

About 0.08 seconds (elapsed). The complexity is O(2^n), so each extra object
doubles the work.

## Dynamic programming

```{r}
knapsack_dynamic(knapsack_objects[1:500, ], W = 3500)
```

```{r}
system.time(knapsack_dynamic(knapsack_objects[1:500, ], W = 3500))
```

**Question: How much time does it take to run the algorithm for n = 500 objects?**

About 0.30 seconds. The complexity is O(W·n), so it grows linearly in n and in W.
It scales far better than brute force.

## Greedy heuristic

```{r}
greedy_knapsack(knapsack_objects[1:800, ], W = 3500)
```

```{r}
set.seed(42)
n <- 1000000
big <- data.frame(w = sample(1:4000, n, replace = TRUE),
                  v = runif(n, 0, 10000))
system.time(greedy_knapsack(big, W = 3500))
```

**Question: How much time does it take to run the algorithm for n = 1,000,000 objects?**

About 0.04 seconds. The complexity is O(n log n), dominated by sorting on the
value/weight ratio. The trade-off is it comsumes less memory.

## Profiling and optimization

```{r, eval = FALSE}
profvis::profvis({
  greedy_knapsack(big, W = 3500)
})
```

I compared the original and the optimized `greedy_knapsack` on 1,000,000
items with `bench::mark()`:

| Version   | Median time | Memory allocated | GCs |
|-----------|-------------|------------------|-----|
| Original  | 32.2 ms     | 36.4 MB          | 2   |
| Optimized | 26.3 ms     | 26.7 MB          | 1   |

**Question: What performance gain could you get by trying to improve your code?**

The optimized version is about 1.2 times faster and allocates about 27% less
memory.

## Rcpp

Implementation in C++ with Rcpp
`fast = TRUE` (default `FALSE`).

```{r rcpp-bench}
res <- bench::mark(
  r    = knapsack_dynamic(knapsack_objects[1:500, ], W = 3500, fast = FALSE),
  rcpp = knapsack_dynamic(knapsack_objects[1:500, ], W = 3500, fast = TRUE),
  iterations = 20
)
res
t_r   <- as.numeric(res$median[1]) * 1000  # ms
t_cpp <- as.numeric(res$median[2]) * 1000  # ms
```

**Question: What performance gain could you get by using Rcpp and C++?**

The Rcpp version had a median time of `r round(t_cpp, 1)` ms versus
`r round(t_r, 1)` ms for the R version, about `r round(t_r / t_cpp)` times
faster. The loops run as compiled code instead of interpreted R. Both versions
return identical results.
